title: Enterprise reserved SKU messaging cheatsheet
content:
Purpose:
Quick reference for enterprise AE/PM teams to position Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPU capacity) during procurement and legal review cycles. Focus: SLAs, isolation guarantees, predictable throughput, and procurement-ready language that speeds contract velocity.

Audience:
- Enterprise buyers (platform teams, infra architects, procurement)
- Technical buyers evaluating performance/cost tradeoffs
- Legal and security reviewers asking for isolation, data handling, and uptime commitments

Topline message (1-liner):
Dedicated capacity from Redwood delivers predictable throughput and production-grade SLAs with isolation controls that make inference procurement as reliable as other core infra contracts.

Three buyer pains we address:
1) Unpredictable token spend and performance when using public/shared inference endpoints.
2) Risk of noisy neighbors and data commingling in multi-tenant offerings.
3) Procurement/legal friction around uptime, incident response, and auditability for regulated workloads.

Pillars & supporting proof points:
- Predictable throughput and latency
  - Commitment: SLO-backed p95 and p99 latency windows for configured model/SKU bundles (sample: p95 < 120ms for short-response gen on r-infer-m60-8).
  - Observable: Per-SKU dashboards with token-level throughput and latency histograms.
  - Procurement ask: Include a target throughput floor and a credits/refund schedule if throughput targets are not met for two consecutive quarters.

- Isolation & data boundary guarantees
  - Commitment: Dedicated GPU pools per customer; no cross-tenant KV/prefix caching by default.
  - Controls: VPC peering or Private mode; customer-managed KMS for keys and optional HSM integrations.
  - Procurement ask: Clause that prohibits co-locating untrusted tenants in the same reserved pool and requires audit logs showing isolation enforcement.

- SLA and operational readiness
  - Typical SLA: 99.95% availability for Dedicated endpoints; optional premium SLA up to 99.99% for multi-region reserved deployments.
  - Incident response: 1-hour P1 response, quarterly incident reviews, and an RCA delivery commitment window.
  - Procurement ask: Specify credits for downtime and require defined on-call escalation contacts and SLO reporting cadence.

- Capacity planning and bursting
  - Offerings: Base reserved capacity + configured burst credits for traffic surges to avoid dropped requests.
  - Autoscaling policy: Configurable min/max pools, predictable billing for burst usage.
  - Procurement ask: Include a burst budget clause and transparent surge billing caps for the first 90 days post-go-live.

Competitive positioning (short notes for quick rebuttals):
- General cloud GPU infra vendors (managed endpoints + infra):
  - Strengths of competitors: Deep infra discounts, familiarity, integrated cloud tooling.
  - Redwood counter: We provide inference-optimized runtime (better per-token cost and latency), explicit model-serving features (KV caching, prefix reuse), and SLA constructs tailored to inference, not generic VM uptime.

- Public LLM API providers (pay-as-you-go):
  - Strengths: Fast onboarding, simple billing.
  - Redwood counter: For enterprise scale, pay-as-you-go leads to unpredictable cost and contention. Dedicated capacity reduces unit cost, guarantees throughput, and supports compliance controls.

- Self-hosted open-source inference stacks:
  - Strengths: Full control, potential cost savings at very large scale.
  - Redwood counter: Operating complexity is non-trivial (kernel/runtime tuning, NVMe/KV cache ops, patching). We offer a managed plane with transparent ops SLAs and optional private deployments for customers who need on-prem.

Procurement-ready language snippets (copy/paste):
- SLA snippet: "Redwood will maintain a monthly availability SLA of 99.95% for Dedicated endpoints. If availability falls below SLA in any billing month, Customer will receive service credits equal to 5% of the monthly commitment for each 0.1% below the SLA, up to a maximum of 100% of monthly fees for that month."
- Isolation snippet: "Dedicated capacity will be provisioned as customer-dedicated GPU pools. Redwood will not co-locate third-party tenant workloads in Customer-assigned pools and will provide access logs demonstrating pool assignments on quarterly request."
- Data protection snippet: "Customer data processed on Dedicated capacity will be segregated and encrypted at rest using Customer-managed KMS keys where requested. Logs and telemetry retention windows will be configurable to support regulatory requirements."

Negotiation playbook (signals and concessions):
- If buyer pushes hard on price: Trade on term length and commit level (12–36 month reserved discounts) and offer an introductory burst credit buffer.
- If buyer demands higher SLA: Offer multi-AZ reserved pools with active-standby across regions for an uplifted price; provide a precise target and RCAs.
- If buyer insists on on-prem: Move to Private deployment conversation; prepare an SOW that lays out HW sizing, install timeline (typically 6–12 weeks), and higher M&O fees.

Redlines to expect from legal/security:
- Data residency: Customers will request region-locking & contractual residency guarantees. Offer region-specific Dedicated pools and contract language for data residency.
- Subprocessor & audit clauses: Be prepared to provide subprocessor lists and SOC2-like reports; for larger customers provide limited-scope on-site audits or a security questionnaire.
- Indemnity/limitation: Push for standard limitation of liability; avoid open-ended guarantees for model outputs.

Technical appendix (for AE/SE talking points):
- Throughput determinism: Explain how runtime batching, KV/prefix cache locality, and dedicated memory allocation reduce variance versus shared endpoints. Use a simple slide: shared < variance < dedicated.
- Predictable unit economics: Show a simple cost-per-token model comparing hosted PAYG vs Reserved at sample 2.5B token/month workload.
- Monitoring and telemetry: Outline available metrics (tokens/sec, queue depth, per-SKU p95/p99 latencies, cache hit rates) and how they map to SLA compliance.

Trial & onboarding suggestions to accelerate procurement:
- Offer a short-term pilot (90 days) with a small reserved pool + capped burst. Include an evaluation checklist for performance and a runbook for failover testing.
- Provide a pre-baked security pack (config templates for VPC, KMS, logging) to reduce legal/security review loops.
- Include a named solution-engineer in the SOW for first 60–90 days to assure ramp and performance tuning.

Open questions (internal notes):
- Standardize numeric SLA language across SKUs and publish a simple table for sales kits.
- Define a fixed set of burst credit SKUs to avoid custom billing exceptions.
- Clarify thresholds for credit/penalty calculations that legal is comfortable codifying.

Quick call checklist (for AE/SE prepping a deal call):
- Confirm buyer pain: cost variance, latency incidents, compliance needs.
- Which models/seq lengths? Size the reserved pool accordingly.
- Preferred region and KMS requirements?
- Procurement timeline and decision-makers? (procurement, security, infra, legal)
